title: s- and p-Block Elements
tagline: Formative study: how electronic configuration governs the trends across the periods and down the groups, and why the first element of each group behaves so differently.

overview.intro: The official CBSE document includes this topic in the syllabus but assesses it only formatively, to reinforce understanding without adding to the summative examination. The subject is periodicity made concrete: the s-block metals of groups 1 and 2 and the p-block elements of groups 13 to 18 are studied through their electronic configurations, their atomic and ionic radii, their ionisation enthalpies and their hydration enthalpies, and the physical and chemical trends that follow from them. Particular attention is paid to the unique behaviour of the first element of each group, whose small size, high electronegativity and (for the second period) the absence of d orbitals make it differ sharply from its congeners, and to the diagonal relationships that make lithium resemble magnesium and beryllium resemble aluminium.

learningOutcomes: Write the electronic configurations of the s- and p-block elements and relate them to their positions in the periodic table.
Describe the trends in atomic and ionic radii, ionisation enthalpy and hydration enthalpy across periods and down groups.
Explain the anomalous behaviour of the first element of each group and the diagonal relationships it produces.
Predict physical and chemical properties of s- and p-block elements from their position and justify the prediction.
Distinguish the ionic lattice argument for the alkali metal chlorides from the intermolecular-force argument for the hydrogen halides, and explain why HF is the highest melting hydrogen halide.

learn.title: The s-block elements: trends down groups 1 and 2

blocks.text: The s-block consists of groups 1 and 2, whose elements fill the s subshell: group 1 has the configuration ns¹ and is called the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium), while group 2 has ns² and is called the alkaline earth metals (beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium). Both families are soft metals with low melting points, strong reducing agents and a strong tendency to lose their valence electrons to form +1 and +2 ions. Down each group the atomic radius increases because a new shell is added at each step, so the outer electron is held less tightly: ionisation enthalpy falls, the metals become more reactive, and the character of the bonding in the compounds becomes more ionic. The density rises down group 1 until potassium, which is lighter than water for structural reasons, and melting points fall down group 1 because the metallic bond weakens as the atoms grow larger.

Hydration enthalpy runs in the opposite direction to atomic size. When an ion dissolves it is surrounded by a shell of water molecules oriented with their oxygen atoms towards the positive charge, and the energy released is the hydration enthalpy. Smaller ions with higher charge density attract water more strongly, so Li⁺ has a much larger hydration enthalpy than Na⁺, which is larger than K⁺, and the trend explains why the lithium salts of many anions are hydrated crystals while the caesium salts are usually not. It also explains the order of solubility and the order of thermal stability of the carbonates and nitrates: the larger the cation, the more stable the carbonate, so lithium carbonate decomposes on heating while barium carbonate does not. Down group 2 the same reasoning applies with doubly charged ions, and because M²⁺ ions are both smaller and more highly charged than the group 1 ions, group 2 compounds are generally less soluble and their hydroxides less strong as bases than those of group 1.

learn.title: The unique behaviour of the first element of each group

blocks.text: The first element of each period differs from the rest of its group for three connected reasons: its atoms are exceptionally small, it has no d orbitals in its valence shell, and the small size of its atom and ion gives unusually high electronegativity and polarising power. Nitrogen, for example, forms a triple bond and exists as N₂, whereas the heavier group 15 elements prefer three single bonds and form P₄; boron forms volatile covalent boron trichloride while aluminium forms an ionic lattice; carbon dioxide is a gas built from pπ-pπ multiple bonds whereas silicon dioxide is a giant covalent network solid with a much higher melting point. Because the second period has only the 2s and 2p orbitals available, its atoms cannot expand their octet, so they form a maximum of four bonds, and multiple bonding with nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine is far more common there than further down the group.

The small size of the first elements also produces the diagonal relationships. Elements placed diagonally in adjacent groups — lithium and magnesium, beryllium and aluminium, boron and silicon — have similar charge-to-radius ratios, and so similar polarising powers, that they behave alike. Lithium forms only the oxide Li₂O on burning in air, like magnesium, rather than the peroxide or superoxide formed by the heavier alkali metals; lithium carbonate and lithium nitrate both decompose on heating rather than melting, again like magnesium; beryllium, like aluminium, forms a covalent chloride and is passivated by concentrated nitric acid; and boron, like silicon, forms acidic oxides and borates rather than basic ones. The diagonal relationship is the clearest illustration that position in the table, not merely group membership, determines chemical behaviour.

learn.title: The p-block elements: trends across the periods and down the groups

blocks.text: The p-block occupies groups 13 to 18 and fills the p subshell from p¹ to p⁶. Across a period from left to right the atomic radius decreases as the nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, ionisation enthalpy increases, electronegativity increases and metallic character falls, so each period runs from a strongly metallic element (aluminium) through metalloids (boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium) to strongly non-metallic fluorine and the noble gases. Down a group the radius increases, ionisation enthalpy falls and metallic character rises, which is why group 13 begins with the metalloid boron, continues with the metal aluminium, and ends with thallium; groups 15 to 17 run from non-metals through metalloids to metals, with the inert pair effect making the lower oxidation states of the heavier elements more stable.

The chemical properties of the p-block follow the same reasoning. Boron forms only covalent compounds and its halides are electron-deficient Lewis acids that accept an electron pair; aluminium, with a filled d shell absent but a larger size, forms mainly ionic compounds yet its chloride is covalent and dimeric because the small, highly charged Al³⁺ ion polarises chloride strongly. Carbon and silicon both show tetravalence, but carbon catenates strongly and builds chains and rings while silicon prefers the silicon-oxygen bond, which is why the silicates and silicones are built from SiO₄ units. Nitrogen has a stable triple bond and a basic lone pair, phosphorus forms the P₄ molecule and shows +3 and +5 states, oxygen supports hydrogen bonding throughout the second period, and fluorine is the most electronegative element with only one common oxidation state, −1.

items.text: Explain why the melting point of the group 1 chlorides falls from LiCl to CsCl while that of the hydrides of group 17 falls in the opposite sense.
items.note: The alkali metal chlorides are ionic lattices, and down the group the cation grows larger, lowering the lattice energy and therefore the melting point: LiCl 883 K, NaCl 1074 K... the actual measured order rises slightly with lattice geometry, so the lattice-energy argument is applied to the enthalpy of formation rather than raw melting point, where crystal structure also matters. The hydrogen halides, by contrast, are molecular solids whose melting points depend on van der Waals forces, which strengthen with molecular size and mass, so HF > HCl < HBr < HI with hydrogen bonding making HF the highest of all.

items.text: Explain why the melting points of the chlorides rise from LiCl to NaCl but then the trend in the hydrogen halides is different: why is HF higher than HCl, and why does the order become HCl < HBr < HI after that?
items.note: The alkali metal chlorides are ionic, so their thermal behaviour is set primarily by the lattice energy of the crystal, not just a single melting point, and for these salts the lattice energy argument is usually applied to the enthalpy of formation rather than to the raw melting point, because the measured melting order is affected by the particular crystal structures adopted. The hydrogen halides, by contrast, are discrete molecules held together as a solid only by van der Waals forces, so their melting points rise with molecular size and hence with the strength of the dispersion forces: HCl is lower than HBr which is lower than HI. HF is the exception because hydrogen bonding, a much stronger intermolecular force, holds its molecules together in the solid, so HF melts higher than the others despite being the lightest molecule.

blocks.caption: Period 3 p-block: how properties change across the period

blocks.text: Almost every property taught in this topic follows from two competing quantities: the nuclear charge, which pulls electrons in, and the number of shells, which pushes them out. Across a period only the charge rises, so the atom contracts and holds its electrons more tightly; down a group a whole shell is added each time, so the atom expands and the outer electrons are lost more easily. Hydration enthalpy follows the charge density that results, and chemical behaviour follows the ionisation enthalpy, the electronegativity and the availability of orbitals. Learning the trends as consequences of this one competition is far more reliable than memorising a table of numbers, and it is also the method the examination expects: a good answer states the trend, gives the electronic reason, and then draws the chemical consequence.

questions.prompt: Which property increases down group 1 of the periodic table?
questions.explanation: Down group 1 each element adds a whole new shell of electrons, so the atom grows larger and the atomic radius increases. Ionisation enthalpy, electronegativity and hydration enthalpy all fall as the outer electron is held less tightly and the charge density of the ion decreases.

questions.prompt: The diagonal relationship of lithium is with:
questions.explanation: Lithium lies in group 1 period 2 and magnesium in group 2 period 3; their ions have similar charge-to-radius ratios, so they resemble each other chemically. Lithium forms only the normal oxide and its carbonate decomposes on heating, just as magnesium does, unlike the heavier alkali metals.

questions.prompt: Why does the second period differ most from the rest of its groups?
options: It has the highest nuclear charge
It has no d orbitals available for bonding
It is the most metallic period
questions.answer: It has no d orbitals available for bonding
questions.explanation: The second period elements have only the 2s and 2p orbitals in their valence shell, so they cannot expand beyond an octet and form a maximum of four bonds. This absence of d orbitals, together with their very small size, is why nitrogen forms N₂ rather than an allotrope like P₄ and why silicon dioxide is a network solid while carbon dioxide is a molecular gas.

questions.prompt: The hydration enthalpy of the alkali metal ions falls in the order:
questions.explanation: Hydration enthalpy depends on charge density: the smaller the ion, the more strongly it attracts the oriented water molecules. Lithium is the smallest alkali metal ion and therefore the most heavily hydrated, while caesium is the largest and least hydrated, which also explains why lithium salts are commonly hydrated crystals and caesium salts generally are not.

questions.prompt: The electronic configuration of the alkaline earth metals is __________.
questions.explanation: Group 2 elements have two electrons in their outermost s subshell, written ns²; they achieve stability by losing both to form M²⁺ ions with a noble gas configuration.

questions.prompt: The p-block of the periodic table comprises groups __________.
questions.explanation: The p-block spans groups 13 to 18, filling the p subshell from p¹ to p⁶ across each period; it is the only block containing metals, metalloids and non-metals together.

questions.prompt: Explain why the ionisation enthalpy of caesium is lower than that of lithium.
questions.answer: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from an isolated gaseous atom. Caesium has six occupied shells and its valence electron is far from the nucleus, shielded by many inner shells of electrons, so the effective attraction on it is weak and little energy removes it. Lithium has only two shells, its 2s electron is close to the nucleus and shielded by only one inner shell, so it is held much more tightly. The result is 520 kJ mol⁻¹ for lithium against 376 kJ mol⁻¹ for caesium, and the same reasoning explains the increase in atomic radius and the increase in reactivity down the group.
questions.explanation: The answer must invoke both the greater number of shells and the greater shielding, since either alone is incomplete; the trend is stated first, the electronic cause second.

questions.prompt: What is a diagonal relationship, and why does it occur?
questions.answer: A diagonal relationship is the chemical similarity between an element and the element located diagonally below it in the adjacent group, such as lithium and magnesium, beryllium and aluminium, or boron and silicon. It arises because the charge-to-radius ratio, and hence the polarising power, of the two ions is very similar: moving one step to the right increases the charge while moving one step down increases the size, and the two effects roughly cancel. The similarity therefore shows up in properties that depend on polarising power, such as the covalent character of chlorides, the thermal stability of carbonates and nitrates, and the amphoteric or acidic nature of the oxides.
questions.explanation: Marks go to the mechanism, not the list: the diagonal step increases charge and increases size at the same time, so the charge density stays comparable.

questions.prompt: Describe the trends in atomic radius and ionisation enthalpy across the third period from sodium to argon, and explain the two irregularities that occur in the ionisation enthalpy values.
questions.answer: Across period 3 the atomic radius falls steadily from sodium at 186 pm to argon at about 71 pm, because each successive element has one more proton while the new electron enters the same third shell, so the effective nuclear attraction on the outer electrons increases and the shell contracts. Ionisation enthalpy correspondingly rises from 496 kJ mol⁻¹ for sodium to about 1581 kJ mol⁻¹ for argon. Two irregularities interrupt the rise. First, aluminium has a slightly lower first ionisation enthalpy than magnesium: magnesium has a completed 3s² subshell whose electrons are lower in energy and well shielded, while the electron removed from aluminium is a 3p electron that is higher in energy and only partly shielded, so it leaves more easily. Second, sulphur has a lower value than phosphorus: phosphorus has the exactly half-filled 3p³ configuration with one electron in each orbital and maximum exchange energy, whereas sulphus has a paired electron in one 3p orbital, and the repulsion within that pair makes the electron easier to remove. Both irregularities are therefore consequences of subshell structure rather than exceptions to the underlying trend.
questions.explanation: A complete answer states the general trend with its electronic cause and then names both irregularities with the half-filled and fully filled subshell arguments; forgetting the aluminium-magnesium dip is the commonest lost mark.

questions.prompt: Compare the chemistry of beryllium with that of aluminium, and use the observations that beryllium is not attacked by alkalis while magnesium is, and that beryllium chloride is a covalent dimer, to discuss the diagonal relationship and the consequences of high polarising power.
questions.answer: Beryllium in group 2 period 2 and aluminium in group 13 period 3 are diagonal neighbours with similar charge-to-radius ratios, and their chemistry converges in four respects. Both form covalent rather than ionic halides: BeCl₂ is a covalent polymer that dimerises to Be₂Cl₄ with bridging chlorines, exactly as Al₂Cl₆ does, because the small, doubly charged Be²⁺ and triply charged Al³⁺ ions polarise the large chloride ions so strongly that electron density is shared rather than transferred. Both oxides are amphoteric rather than basic, dissolving in acids and in alkalis. Both metals are rendered passive by concentrated nitric acid, which builds an oxide film. And both form polymeric hydrides, BeH₂ and the aluminohydrides, with bridging hydrogen atoms. The observation that beryllium is not attacked by alkalis while magnesium is follows from the same polarising power: Be²⁺ is so small and charge-dense that it forms the beryllate anion only under forcing conditions, whereas the larger Mg²⁺ gives the simpler amphoteric Mg(OH)₂ that dissolves in alkali. The practical consequence of this diagonal relationship is that beryllium compounds must be handled as if they were aluminium compounds, not as typical group 2 compounds, and their covalency is the single fact from which every other similarity follows.
questions.explanation: The examiner looks for the unifying idea — charge density — applied consistently to bonding, oxide character and reactivity, rather than a list of matched observations.
